title: How to train staff on phone orders
seoTitle: Train staff on phone orders | ROAL
description: Train staff on phone orders with simple scripts, clear order checks, and a phone setup that helps a busy restaurant keep service moving.
question: How do I train staff to take phone orders without messing up service?
answer: Train staff to take phone orders by giving them a short script, a clear order checklist, and a simple handoff rule for allergies, catering, complaints, and manager requests. Practice with real menu items, then review a few calls each shift so mistakes get corrected fast. If the phone is still too busy, an AI phone host like ROAL can take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu and send clean tickets to the kitchen.
summary: You’ll know how to train staff to take phone orders with less stress, fewer mistakes, and clearer handoffs.
intro:
Training new staff to take phone orders starts with one goal: keep the line moving without losing the order. The best training is short, specific, and tied to your menu, not a big speech they will forget after the rush.

For a pizza shop, deli, takeout counter, or family restaurant, phone orders should follow the same steps every time. That means a script, a repeat-back, a ready-time check, and a rule for when to pass the call to a manager or staff member.

sections.h2: What should every phone order follow from hello to ticket?
sections.body:
Start with a simple flow that every new staff member can repeat. Keep it the same on day one and day thirty. If the flow changes every shift, mistakes pile up.

Use this as your basic order path:
1. Answer with your restaurant name.
2. Ask whether the caller wants pickup or delivery.
3. Take the items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
4. Confirm the caller’s name and phone number.
5. Give the ready time.
6. Read the order back once.
7. Send it to the kitchen or write it clearly for the expo line.

A good script line sounds like this: “Thanks for calling Mama Rosa’s. Is this pickup or delivery?” Then: “Can I get your order, please?”

Put the same checklist near the phone and on the prep counter. For example, a deli cashier should always capture sandwich choice, bread, toppings, chips or sides, and any special instructions. If your menu has common add-ons, list them on the sheet so staff do not have to guess.

If you use ROAL, it follows that same order flow on the phone and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That can help when the front counter is busy and new staff are still learning the menu.

sections.h2: How do you teach new hires the menu fast?
sections.body:
New staff do not need to memorize your whole menu on day one. They need to know the items that are ordered most often, plus the changes customers ask for most. Teach in pieces, not in a giant dump of information.

Try a three-step training block:
1. Show the top 10 items and common sizes.
2. Review the most common modifiers, like extra cheese, no onions, well done, or sauce on the side.
3. Practice with 5 fake calls using real menu items.

A useful exercise is to read a sample order out loud and have the trainee write it the way the kitchen needs it. Example: “Two large plain pies, one with extra cheese, one with half pepperoni, and one Caesar salad with dressing on the side.” Ask them to repeat it back cleanly before they call it done.

Use a small cheat sheet with these columns:

| Menu item | Common sizes | Common modifiers | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pizza | Small, medium, large | Extra cheese, light sauce | Ask crust style if needed |
| Sandwiches | Half, whole | Toasted, no mayo | Confirm bread type |
| Plates | Single, combo | Extra sauce, no onions | Check side choices |

That kind of sheet helps new staff stay calm. It also makes it easier to train someone different tomorrow if your schedule changes often. Owners who want a phone-specific version can also look at [Phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates).

sections.h2: What do staff need to ask every caller so orders are accurate?
sections.body:
Accuracy comes from asking the same questions in the same order. New staff often get nervous and skip one step, then the kitchen has to guess. Make the questions short and direct.

Here is a solid set for most restaurants:
- What would you like to order?
- Is that pickup or delivery?
- What size do you want?
- Any toppings, sides, or modifiers?
- What name should I put on the order?
- What is the best phone number?
- What time would you like it ready?

Say the questions the same way each time. For example: “What size would you like?” is better than asking three different ways in one call. If your menu has sold-out items, tell staff to stop suggesting them and offer the next best option.

Train them to read back the full order before hanging up. A simple script line helps: “Let me read that back to make sure I got it right.” Then repeat the items, size, modifiers, phone number, and ready time.

If the caller sounds unsure, staff should slow down and ask one question at a time. That matters more during dinner rush than perfect speed. A clean order is faster than a corrected one.

ROAL does this automatically on calls from the restaurant’s live menu, and it does not offer items marked sold out. It can also speak the caller’s language, which helps when your front-of-house team is short or busy.

sections.h2: When should staff hand the call to a manager?
sections.body:
Not every call should stay with the first person who answers it. Some calls need judgment, and your staff should know exactly when to stop and pass them along.

Make these the clear handoff calls:
- Catering requests
- Complaint calls
- Allergy-sensitive questions
- Manager requests
- Large or unusual orders
- Anything the staff member cannot answer confidently

Give them a phrase they can use without sounding stiff: “I want to make sure you get the right answer, so I’m going to get my manager for you.” That keeps the caller calm and avoids guessing.

You can also train a quick summary note before transfer. For example: “Caller wants 18 trays for Friday, asked about gluten-free options, callback number ends in 4421.” That saves time when the manager picks up.

This is one of the best places to use an AI phone host for restaurants. ROAL sends tough calls to staff with a summary instead of trying to fake an answer. That means the team sees the issue fast and can handle it the right way.

If you want a full owner-level handoff policy, [What calls should reach the manager](/blog/restaurant-manager-phone-escalations) is a good companion read.

sections.h2: How do you keep phone training from falling apart on a busy night?
sections.body:
Most phone training falls apart when the rush starts. The fix is not more theory. The fix is a short routine that fits the shift you already have.

Use a 10-minute pre-shift drill:
1. Review today’s sold-out items.
2. Read three common orders out loud.
3. Practice one pickup, one delivery, and one complaint handoff.
4. Remind staff who answers the phone first.
5. Check who can take notes and who can run tickets.

A simple phone board helps too. Put the current hour’s most ordered items, any 86’d items, and the manager name on one sheet near the register. That way a new hire is not hunting for information while the phone rings.

Here is a useful example. Say your average phone order is $28. If a staff member fumbles one call and the order has to be re-taken, you spend extra time and may lose the sale. Plug in your own average ticket and your own call volume to see why the process matters.

For busy nights, some owners also forward calls when the counter gets overloaded. Phone forwarding codes vary by carrier and system, so confirm with your provider and test it. [Call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) can help you check the basics before you set it up.

The bigger point is simple: train for the rush you actually have, not the quiet hour you wish you had.

sections.h2: How can a restaurant owner use phone tech without losing control?
sections.body:
Good phone training does not mean you give up control. It means you decide which calls the staff handles, which calls go to a manager, and which calls can be answered by a phone host when the team is slammed.

A practical setup looks like this:
- Staff answers normal orders when the dining room is calm.
- A phone host handles routine pickup and delivery orders from the live menu when you want backup.
- Manager-only calls still go to a person.
- The kitchen sees clean tickets, not scribbled notes.

ROAL is set up from a restaurant website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name and city. The owner can test-call it in the browser before going live, then forward the restaurant’s existing number to it if they want. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

It also avoids one big training mistake: never let a new hire take payment card numbers over the phone. Payment stays where the restaurant already takes it, at pickup or through the normal process you use.

takeaways: Train phone orders with one clear script, not a loose guess.
Teach the menu in pieces: top items, common modifiers, and sold-out items.
Use a hard handoff rule for catering, complaints, allergies, and manager calls.
Read orders back before hanging up and send them to the kitchen cleanly.
Confirm call forwarding with your carrier before you rely on it.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to train staff to take phone orders?
faq.a: Use a one-page script and a short practice loop. Have each new hire answer the same way, ask the same order questions, and read back the order before they hang up. Then review a few calls after service so you can correct mistakes while the details are fresh.

faq.q: What should new restaurant staff ask on every phone order?
faq.a: They should ask for pickup or delivery, the items, size, modifiers, the caller’s name, the best phone number, and the ready time. Those questions cover the order and reduce back-and-forth later. If the caller changes the order, staff should repeat the updated version before finishing.

faq.q: How do I train staff to handle difficult phone calls?
faq.a: Give them a clear handoff rule. Allergy questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests should go to a manager with a short summary. A simple line like, “I want to make sure you get the right answer, so I’m getting my manager,” keeps the call calm.

faq.a: Yes, especially when your team is short or still learning. ROAL answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, confirms the order, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It still sends tricky calls to staff, so your team keeps control where it matters.
